cards.explanation: The answer is that Job justified himself rather than God. That's the reason the text gives. Elihu burned with anger against Job "…for justifying himself rather than God…" (Job 32:2). Elihu is Barachel's son, a Buzite, and he had been waiting to speak to Job (Job 32:4). Now the waiting is over.

The answer is True. Elihu's anger doesn't stop at Job. He also "…burned with anger against Job’s three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him." (Job 32:3). Elihu is handing out anger like free cookie samples, friends, one for Job and one for each of the three.

The answer is older. "…Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he." (Job 32:4). He kept waiting until he saw that the three men had no further reply, and then his anger was kindled (Job 32:5). That's a lot of patience for one man.

The answer is True. Elihu says, "I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know." (Job 32:6). He's being honest about why he stayed quiet. I think that took some nerve to say out loud.

The answer is the breath of the Almighty. Elihu says, "…there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding." (Job 32:8). He's saying understanding comes from God, not just from gray hair.

The answer is old. Elihu says, "It is not only the old who are wise, or the elderly who understand justice." (Job 32:9). He's pushing back on the idea that wisdom comes only with age. Notice he says "not only," so he isn't throwing the old out, friends.

The answer is not with the friends' arguments. Elihu says, "…Job has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your arguments." (Job 32:14). He plans to come at Job with his own words. He's not borrowing anybody's notes.

The answer is False. Elihu asks, "Must I wait, now that they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply?" (Job 32:16). Then he says, "I too will answer; yes, I will declare what I know." (Job 32:17). His waiting is over.

The answer is a wineskin about to burst. Elihu says, "…my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin." (Job 32:19). He's so full of words he feels ready to pop. I think anybody who's held in a long story knows that feeling.

The answer is False. Elihu says, "I will be partial to no one, nor will I flatter any man." (Job 32:21). He's saying he won't play favorites. He's going to say what he knows, no matter who it lands on.
